The diagnostic yield, using this technology, is superior to conventional bronchoscopy techniques and is discussed. The respiratory motion of the airways, lung, and nodule hysteresis creates unique challenges for targeting the lesion. Use of fluoroscopy and radial-probe ultrasound provide meaningful information and additional confirmation with difficult lesions. We continue to evolve in our understanding of how best to utilize the technology, modify diagnostic tools, and improve next-generation platforms. Even so, EMN bronchoscopy has changed the landscape of tissue acquisition for peripheral lung lesions. This review provides important principles and practical aspects of pre-procedure preparation, assessment of airway-lesion relationships, procedural workflow and performance, and points for consideration when contemplating acquisition of an EMN system. The future is in development of intuitive platforms that will allow consistent targeting with higher accuracy so ablation techniques could be performed safely via the endobronchial approach.

METHODS: Narrative review of electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy technology, workflows, CT planning protocols, registration and navigation methods, and commercially available platforms (superDimension, Veran SPiN, Archimedes). The authors describe practical implementation, imaging requirements, planning steps, and procedural setup.

RESULTS: As a review article, no primary data analyses or comparative outcomes are reported. The article summarizes that EMN bronchoscopy enables real-time tracking and virtual bronchoscopy guidance derived from thin-slice CT, discusses sources of error (e.g., electromagnetic field distortion, CT-to-body divergence, respiratory motion), and outlines workflows for registration and navigation with different platforms. It notes reported diagnostic yield in early human studies approaching 70% and describes adjuncts such as fluoroscopy, radial-probe endobronchial ultrasound, and cone-beam CT for lesion confirmation.

steps: Obtain high-resolution chest CT and reconstruct 3D model with navigation software (e.g., Archimedes).
Identify an optimal POE on the airway wall and an avascular path to the nodule.
Confirm feasibility relative to nearby critical structures on CT (vessels, heart, esophagus).
Insert bronchoscope and navigate to the predetermined POE under navigation guidance.
Puncture the airway wall with a coring needle or Fle XNeedle to create the initial opening.
Dilate the puncture with a balloon catheter to establish a tunnel entrance.
Advance a sheath with a blunt dissection stylet through lung parenchyma to the lesion under real-time fluoroscopy/navigation.
Remove the blunt stylet and use forceps, brush, and/or needle aspiration through the sheath to obtain tissue.
Employ multiple sampling tools to maximize representativeness.
Monitor for pneumothorax; obtain chest imaging if symptomatic and manage with observation or chest tube as indicated.
Manage hemorrhage with local measures; escalate to vascular/surgical intervention if major vessel injury occurs.
Use aseptic technique; consider antibiotics per local protocol to prevent infection; monitor for bronchial injury.
Working channel ≥2.0 mm when using only Fle XNeedle and balloon catheter.
Working channel ≥2.8 mm when using a sheath with Fle XNeedle and balloon catheter.
Identify CT membrane via midline palpation; alternative: 3–4 fingerbreadths above suprasternal notch with neck neutral.
Use large-bore catheter-over-needle (e.g., 14-g) attached to syringe partially filled with saline/water.
Advance at ~45° angle caudally through skin and CT membrane while aspirating; air bubbles confirm entry.
Withdraw needle, leave cannula; connect oxygen tubing.
Deliver oxygen at 10–12 L/min; use Y-connector to allow periodic CO₂ release.
Prep anterior neck from mandible angle to sternal notch; maintain sterile technique; position with mandible anteriorly displaced.
Stabilize larynx with thumb and long finger; use index finger to palpate and reidentify CT membrane throughout.
Make a 2 cm midline vertical skin incision over CT membrane, staying strictly in midline to avoid anterior jugular veins.
Palpate CT membrane through incision and make a horizontal incision in the lower half of the membrane.
Insert cricoid hook and apply gentle upward traction on cricoid; avoid traction on thyroid to protect vocal folds.
Dilate cephalocaudally using Trousseau dilator or Kelly clamp to enlarge the opening.
Insert tested tracheostomy or endotracheal tube (outer diameter ≤8 mm) at ~90° between dilator blades; rotate counterclockwise to seat against the neck.
Confirm placement with end-tidal CO₂ return and bilateral breath sounds; secure tube to neck with suture.
Operator at head of bed; identify landmarks and stabilize.
Horizontal stab incision through skin, subcutaneous tissue, and CT membrane to access airway.
Stabilize larynx by hooking cricoid cartilage; apply upward traction.
Insert tracheostomy tube as per standard technique and confirm placement.
Small vertical skin incision over CT membrane; stabilize larynx with nondominant hand.
Advance 18‑gauge needle with syringe through CT membrane; aspirate air to confirm airway entry.
Insert guide wire; remove needle without dislodging wire.
Advance cannula/dilator over wire into airway; seat cannula; remove dilator and wire.
Position needle-knife at 12 o'clock; short activation to incise superficially.
Repeat at 3 and 9 o'clock (and additional quadrants if needed).
Avoid posterior membranous wall to prevent esophageal injury.
Follow with CRE balloon dilation until adequate lumen achieved.
Loop snare at stalk base; tighten to compress blood supply.
Apply EC in brief bursts while tightening until release.
Retrieve specimen with forceps; treat base for hemostasis.
Apply probe tip to target tissue; short activations with suction.
Reassess tissue effect frequently; avoid long activations.
Advance probe ~2 cm distal to scope tip and keep visible.
Aim 1–3 mm from target; short bursts with painting motion.
Coagulate layer-by-layer to achieve devitalized eschar; then mechanically debulk if needed.

steps: General anesthesia; insert dual-cooled radiofrequency catheter via bronchoscope.
Position catheter circumferentially in each main bronchus to ablate vagal fibers at four positions.
Use esophageal balloon with contrast to maintain distance from esophagus and avoid gastric vagal ablation.
Energy selection based on anatomy (26–32 W); radiofrequency activation for 120 s followed by 30 s postcooling.
Administer prophylactic antibiotics and corticosteroids; typical total procedure time ≈74 min.

source.value: Emerging Bronchoscopic Therapies for Lung Disease: Targeted Lung Denervation, Rheoplasty, and Spray Cryotherapy

steps: Under general anesthesia, perform two sessions: right lung then 4–6 weeks later left lung.
Reduce FiO2 to 30% during activations.
Deploy catheter in subsegmental bronchi and advance proximally toward main carina, treating each segment.
Expand electrode to contact mucosa; apply current for 5 s per activation; collapse and move to next site.
Typical duration ≈40 min with ~40–60 activations per side; administer corticosteroids to reduce COPD exacerbation risk.

source.value: Emerging Bronchoscopic Therapies for Lung Disease: Targeted Lung Denervation, Rheoplasty, and Spray Cryotherapy

steps: Insert delivery catheter through bronchoscope; connect to liquid-nitrogen console.
Deliver liquid nitrogen as radial spray with thermocouple feedback to create an ≈10 mm circular ablation zone (depth 0.1–0.5 mm).
Stop ventilation during application and usually deflate endotracheal tube cuff to avoid barotrauma or asphyxia.
Perform three procedures: (1) right lower lobe + right mainstem, (2) left lower lobe + left mainstem, (3) both upper lobes + distal trachea; do not treat right middle lobe.
Mean number of sprays ≈20 per procedure; mean procedure time ≈34 min.

Silicone stent deployment (rigid broncho.source: Endobronchial Silicone Stents for Airway Management
steps: Induce general anesthesia; perform rigid bronchoscopy.
Pre‑treat: mechanical tumor debulking and/or airway dilation as needed.
Measure lesion length endoscopically; confirm CT‑based estimate; select a stent extending 5 mm beyond lesion proximally and distally.
Select diameter based on maximal dilation caliber (trachea 14–16 mm; mainstem 12–13 mm; BI 10–11 mm).
Load stent into introducer; position just distal to lesion; pull back to final position with rigid forceps.
Avoid distal pushing over a pathologic segment; complete expansion with balloon or rigid instruments if needed.
Post‑deploy inspection; schedule follow‑up and annual reassessment/replacement while indicated.

Temporary stent trial for suspected mala.source: Endobronchial Silicone Stents for Airway Management
steps: Place temporary stent as internal splinting.
If clinical improvement: refer for external stenting; consider stent removal.
If no improvement: remove stent; recommend physiotherapy and CPAP.
Position patient supine or ~45° with ipsilateral arm abducted and externally rotated.
Identify the safe triangle: anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, and a line superior to the nipple/submammary fold.
Prep and drape; infiltrate ~20 m L lidocaine to dermis, subcutaneous tissues, intercostal space/periosteum, and parietal pleura.
Aspirate air or fluid during anesthetic to confirm pleural entry; if none, reconfirm with ultrasound.
Make ~2 cm incision over the rib; bluntly dissect through serratus/intercostal muscles along the superior rib border.
Enter pleural space with closed instrument; open while withdrawing to avoid injury and allow egress of air/fluid.
Perform circumferential digital palpation to verify entry and assess adhesions.
Advance tube with Kelly clamp to guide direction (anterior–cranial for air; posterior–caudal for fluid); minimize spillage by proximal clamp as needed.
If significant resistance or kinking is encountered, suspect a false tract and correct before proceeding.
Secure with strong fixation suture (e.g., silk), anchor stitch, and connect to drainage system (typically −20 cm H2O suction for fluid; water seal for pneumothorax unless air evacuation inadequate).
Over-the-wire placement with serial dilation (up to three dilators may be required for catheters up to 32 F).
Lacks digital palpation and manual guidance advantages of the blunt dissection technique.
Select analgesia with NSAIDs and/or opioids; NSAIDs do not impair pleurodesis at 3 months in malignant effusion.
Consider clamping trials for pneumothorax, noting ACCP expert split; digital air-leak devices can hasten removal if no leak is measured.
Outpatient Heimlich valve is reasonable for persistent air leak on water seal when criteria are met (asymptomatic, no subcutaneous emphysema after 14 days, stable pleural space).
For pleural effusion, reported removal thresholds vary widely (<100 to <500 m L/24 h); after lung resection, <5 m L/kg/24 h vs <200 m L/24 h show similar outcomes.
Remove the tube rapidly during positive intrathoracic pressure (patient humming) or during an inspiratory hold on the ventilator.
Perform comprehensive airway-focused preassessment (mouth opening >3 finger breadths, teeth status, modified Mallampati, neck mobility >90°, thyromental distance >3 finger breadths).
Plan anesthesia with general anesthesia/deep sedation and paralytics for therapeutic bronchoscopy; coordinate with anesthesiology.
Select ventilatory support (jet ventilation or controlled/spontaneous assisted ventilation) based on local expertise and patient status; consider ECMO standby for critical obstructions.
Debulk endobronchial tumor using rigid or flexible forceps; consider rigid bronchoscope bevel for coring proximal tumors.
Apply immediate-effect ablative modalities (electrocautery probes, snare/knife; APC; laser) to achieve hemostasis and vaporize tumor.
Maintain FiO2 ≤0.4 and keep active probe tip away from flammable devices to reduce airway fire risk.
Consider photodynamic therapy (PDT) to reduce tumor regrowth in appropriate candidates.
Recognize that brachytherapy and cryotherapy have limited current utilization in many centers.
Use silicone or fully covered hybrid metallic stents to palliate extrinsic compression or maintain patency after debridement in endobronchial CAO.
Prescribe mucociliary clearance therapy (e.g., nebulized hypertonic saline or acetylcysteine) to prevent mucus plugging.
Follow closely and remove stents once significant tumor regression occurs; choose routine or symptom-driven bronchoscopy; use CT to assess stent patency.
Use bronchoscopic palliation to bridge to definitive chemoradiation and/or surgery.

For EBRT in central tumors and in patients with stents, coordinate multidisciplinary planning and adjust dose to minimize toxicity; avoid concurrent chemo-EBRT in high-risk cases and remove stents when feasible.
Indications: at least one mediastinal lesion with short-axis ≥1 cm on thoracic imaging; newly discovered mediastinal lesions; clinical symptoms needing biopsy to establish etiology.
Contraindications: severe cardiopulmonary disease, coagulation disorders, intolerance to anesthesia or endoscopic procedures, psychiatric disorders, severe neurosis.
Supine position; upper airway topical anesthesia with 2% lidocaine.
Conscious sedation with IV midazolam and fentanyl.
Administer oxygen 1–2 L/min; increase if SpO2 <90%.
Continuous monitoring of vital signs and pulse oximetry.
Insert EBUS bronchoscope via nasal route (oral route if nasal passage unsuitable).
Sequentially examine mediastinal and hilar stations per Mountain-Dressler map.
Use Doppler to assess blood supply; measure long and short axes.
Select the most suspicious lesion with relatively lower biopsy risk as target.
Under real-time ultrasound, advance a high-frequency needle-knife via the working channel.
Make a 2–3 mm cut on airway wall adjacent to the target lesion.
Advance into the lesion under ultrasound visualization, avoiding areas with abundant blood flow or massive necrosis; measure insertion depth; withdraw knife.
Advance an appropriate cryoprobe through the window into the lesion under real-time ultrasound.
Activate with nitrous oxide for ~7 s; gently extract probe with frozen specimen attached.
Release specimen by thawing in saline; fix in formalin; send to pathology.
Inspect airway for hemorrhage; apply topical procoagulants as needed.
Obtain chest X-ray or other imaging within 24 hours to detect pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, or mediastinitis.
Follow-up at 24 hours to record symptoms; consider a second follow-up at 1 month.

steps: Size airway using deployment system; choose valve size.
Place valve(s) to occlude all contributing segments.
Confirm air leak reduction at chest drainage device; adjust as needed.

steps: Select spigot size; advance to target segment.
Wedge and seat securely; reassess air leak.
Combine with chemical pleurodesis when appropriate.

Two\u2011slide pull smear technique.source: Rapid Onsite Evaluation and Specimen Preparation
steps: Expel aspirate onto slide A; use slide B to gently spread into two thin smears.
Air‑dry one slide for Diff‑Quik/Giemsa; fix the other in ethanol for Papanicolaou.

ROSE adequacy workflow.source: Rapid Onsite Evaluation and Specimen Preparation
steps: Assess for lymphoid tissue or lesional cells; note artifacts (mucus, ciliated cells, cartilage).
Communicate adequacy to bronchoscopist; adjust passes accordingly.
Allocate additional material to cell block (FFPE) for ancillary testing.

Cell block preparation (FFPE).source: Rapid Onsite Evaluation and Specimen Preparation
steps: Rinse residual material with ~50% ethanol and centrifuge to pellet.
Fix in formalin and embed in paraffin for IHC/FISH/NGS.
Airway inspection; photographic documentation.
BAL and washings via working channel.
Brushings and transbronchial biopsies per protocol.
Suction for mucus plugs, blood/clots.
Support for tumor debulking (mechanical/energy adjuncts), stent deployment, foreign body removal.
Guidance for percutaneous tracheostomy; BLVR tools; bronchial thermoplasty; fiducial placement.
Position patient sitting upright; consider lateral decubitus if unstable.
Perform consent and time-out; mark correct side.
Use ultrasound in real time to localize effusion and optimal intercostal space.
Prep skin with chlorhexidine or betadine; place sterile drape; wear mask and sterile gloves.
Anesthetize skin and intercostal tract with 10 mL of 1% lidocaine using 25-gauge then 22-gauge 2.5-in needle.
Make a small subcutaneous stab incision with #11 scalpel.
Insert needle-with-catheter above the rib into pleural space with continuous aspiration; advance catheter over needle, then withdraw needle.
Drain fluid with one-way syringe and tubing; consider Vacutainer/wall suction cautiously due to possible increased complications.
Monitor symptoms and, if using manometry, stop if Ppl < −20 cmH2O, or if patient develops chest discomfort/cough/shoulder pain, or when no more fluid.
Remove catheter during exhalation; cover site with sterile dressing; consider post-procedure ultrasound; chest radiograph only if suspicion for pneumothorax.
